overview: Baryonyx walkeri was discovered in 1983 by amateur fossil hunter William Walker in a clay pit in Surrey, England — one of the most significant British dinosaur finds of the 20th century. Its preserved stomach contents included both fish scales and the bones of a juvenile Iguanodon, proving it had a dual diet as a fish specialist and an opportunistic predator of terrestrial prey.

A spinosaurid closely related to Suchomimus, Baryonyx had a long narrow skull, 96 interlocking conical teeth and an enormous thumb claw over 31 cm long — the feature that gives it its name ("heavy claw"). The original specimen is now one of the centrepiece displays at the Natural History Museum, London.

fossilSites.name: Weald Clay Formation
fossilSites.note: Early Cretaceous fluvial clay deposit; type locality with the most complete known Baryonyx skeleton.

fossilSites.name: Wessex Formation
fossilSites.note: Barremian fluvial deposits with additional spinosaurid material attributed to Baryonyx or close relatives.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: William Walker found a large claw in a clay pit near Ockley in January 1983; palaeontologists from the NHM then excavated one of the most complete large theropod skeletons known from Europe. Alan Charig and Angela Milner described it formally in 1986, naming the species walkeri in Walker's honour.

articles.title: Diet and feeding
articles.body: The stomach region preserved fish scales of Lepidotes and bones attributed to a juvenile Iguanodon. The narrow snout and conical interlocking teeth are convergent with the skulls of fish-eating crocodilians. The huge thumb claw may have been used to hook fish from water, analogous to grizzly bears.

articles.title: Significance
articles.body: Baryonyx was the first spinosaurid found with stomach contents, providing the first direct dietary evidence for the group. It confirmed that spinosaurids were fish specialists and opportunistic meat-eaters — a feeding ecology subsequently supported by isotope analysis of spinosaurid teeth from multiple species.

fossilRecord.material: Partial skeleton including skull and forelimb material; stomach contents preserve fish scales and young Iguanodon bones.
fossilRecord.completeness: Partial skeleton with direct diet evidence
fossilRecord.paleo: Early Cretaceous wetland and river-influenced environments in southern England.
fossilRecord.evidence: Conical teeth, long jaws, large thumb claw and stomach contents support fish-eating and opportunistic predation.

record.description: Baryonyx walkeri was a baryonychine spinosaurid from the Barremian Weald Clay Formation of England. The holotype is a substantial partial skull and skeleton, and associated gut-region remains provide rare direct evidence of both fish and ornithopod consumption.
facts: The holotype includes much of the skull, vertebral column and limbs, including the enlarged first manual claw.
Fish scales and partly digested iguanodontian bones show a broad carnivorous diet, not exclusive fish-eating.

presentation.heroLead: A crocodile-snouted, heavy-clawed spinosaurid from Early Cretaceous England, and one of the few dinosaurs whose last meal is preserved.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Baryonyx walkeri
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of Baryonyx walkeri, a long-snouted theropod with large hand claws, standing by water
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by Andrey Atuchin. The long, narrow snout and enlarged thumb claw are documented by the holotype; skin texture, colour and the setting are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Baryonyx was a large theropod with a long, low snout lined with many conical teeth, a kinked upper jaw and a large hooked claw, about 31 centimetres along its curve, on the first finger of each hand. The name means 'heavy claw'. It was the first spinosaurid known from a substantial skeleton, and it reshaped how palaeontologists understood the group.

The holotype, found by amateur collector William Walker in a Surrey clay pit in 1983, is roughly two-thirds of a skeleton. Its bones were not fully fused, so the individual may not have been fully grown. Published lengths of around 7.5 to 10 metres and masses of about 1.2 to 1.7 tonnes rest on this one animal.

Fish scales and teeth of the fish Scheenstia, together with partly digested bones of a young iguanodontian, were found in the region of the stomach. This is rare direct evidence of diet in a non-avian dinosaur and shows that Baryonyx took both aquatic and terrestrial prey, whether by hunting or scavenging.
animalHighlights: A long, crocodile-like snout with about twice as many teeth as a typical large theropod.
Gut-region remains preserve fish scales and iguanodontian bones, direct evidence of a mixed carnivorous diet.
The enlarged thumb claw gives the genus its name and is preserved on the holotype.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Fish scales and partly digested iguanodontian bones lay within the holotype's rib cage; whether prey was hunted or scavenged cannot be told.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Hindlimb and pelvic bones show a typical large theropod stance; the robust forelimbs did not bear weight in normal walking.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Estimates derive from the holotype, which may not have been fully grown; larger adults are possible but not documented.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The skeleton constrains proportions well; skin, colour and any soft crest or sail are not preserved.

locality.name: Smokejacks Pit
locality.note: Upper Weald Clay Formation. A working brick-clay pit where William Walker found the large claw in January 1983; the Natural History Museum excavated the skeleton later that year.

presentation.classificationSummary: Baryonyx is a spinosaurid theropod and the name-giving member of Baryonychinae, the branch with more numerous teeth and less specialised jaws than Spinosaurus. Its relationship to Suchomimus is close and sometimes debated, but the two are not treated as synonyms.

related.reason: A very similar baryonychine from Niger, sometimes argued to be extremely close to Baryonyx.
The larger, more aquatic-adapted spinosaurine that Baryonyx helped to reinterpret.
A contemporary Wealden herbivore; a young iguanodontian formed part of the holotype's last meals.

questions.title: Was the holotype fully grown?
questions.copy: Unfused bones suggest it may not have been, so the size of a mature Baryonyx remains open.

questions.title: Which other fossils belong to it?
questions.copy: Isolated teeth and bones from England, Spain and Portugal have been referred to Baryonyx, but many cannot be distinguished from other baryonychines.

questions.title: How did it hunt?
questions.copy: The gut contents show what it ate, not how. Wading and snatching fish is a reasonable inference from the jaws and claws, but it is not directly observed.

review.ageReviewNote: The type locality is Barremian in the Weald Clay Formation.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.note: Partial skull and about two-thirds of the skeleton of a single individual, including the large first-finger claw, with fish scales and iguanodontian bones from the gut region. Found in 1983 and described by Charig and Milner in 1986.

panel.headline: One substantial skeleton with its last meals preserved.
panel.standfirst: Baryonyx is anchored by a single partial skull and skeleton from a Surrey clay pit, the most complete spinosaurid skeleton found in Europe. Referred teeth and bones from elsewhere add little that is diagnostic.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Most skeletal regions are present in one individual, but the skull is incomplete, the tail and parts of the limbs are missing, and no second good skeleton exists.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype includes the front of the snout, parts of the braincase and lower jaw, many teeth, vertebrae from neck to tail, ribs and gastralia, the shoulder girdle and forelimbs with the large claw, the pelvis and much of the hindlimb.
knownRemains.note: The skeleton was partly weathered and disturbed before collection, and much of the tail and the ends of some limbs are missing. Gut-region fish scales and iguanodontian bones are preserved with it.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Conjoined premaxillae, part of the maxilla, nasals, lacrimal, postorbital, braincase elements, parts of both lower jaws and numerous teeth; the middle of the skull is largely missing.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and some caudal vertebrae with ribs, chevrons and gastralia; most of the tail is absent.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Scapula, coracoid, humerus, radius, ulna and hand bones including the large first-finger claw; ilium, pubis, ischium, femur, tibia, fibula and foot bones.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Fish scales and teeth and partly digested iguanodontian bones from the gut region; no skin or feather impressions.

specimenCards.title: NHMUK PV R 9951 · holotype
specimenCards.description: Found by William Walker at Smokejacks Pit in January 1983 and excavated by the Natural History Museum. Described briefly by Charig and Milner in 1986 and in full in 1997, it remains the reference skeleton for Baryonychinae.
specimenCards.meta: Smokejacks Pit · Upper Weald Clay Formation · Natural History Museum, London

specimenCards.title: Isolated teeth and bones
specimenCards.description: Teeth and fragmentary bones from the Isle of Wight, Spain and Portugal have been assigned to Baryonyx or to Baryonyx-like spinosaurids. Most lack the features needed to confirm the genus.
specimenCards.meta: Wessex Formation and Iberian sites · referrals uncertain

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: A partial skull with many conical teeth, most of the postcranial skeleton of one individual, a 31-centimetre hand claw and gut-region fish and dinosaur remains.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A semi-aquatic-capable generalist predator that took both fish and terrestrial prey, with jaw and claw anatomy suited to seizing slippery prey.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Adult size, the complete skull outline, the full tail, soft-tissue features, and which referred Iberian and British fossils truly belong to the genus.
